Ferroptosis mechanism of retinal ganglion cell (RGC) death in glaucoma

The ferroptosis mechanism of retinal ganglion cell (RGC) death in glaucoma. The accumulation of Fe2+ occurs because extracellular ferric ions are taken up through the transferrin (TF) receptor (TFR), reduced to Fe2+ by six-transmembrane epithelial antigen of the prostate 3 (STEAP3), and then transported into the cytoplasm via divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1). Iron autophagy protein nuclear receptor co-activator 4 (NCOA4) releases Fe2+ by degrading ferritin. N-methyl-d-aspartic acid (NMDA) receptors mediate the entry of Fe2+ into the cytoplasm through a signal cascade that activates Dexras1, while FPN is involved in the excretion of Fe2+. Excess intracellular Fe2+ generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) through the Fenton reaction, ultimately leading to the accumulation of lipid peroxides. Glutathione (GSH) peroxidase 4 (GPX4), with the involvement of GSH, reduces toxic phospholipid hydroperoxides (pL-OOH) to non-toxic phospholipid alcohols (PL-OH). Interestingly, both Fe2+ and GPX4 can localize to the mitochondria. Additionally, solute carrier family 7 member 11 (SLC7A11) mediates the transport of glutamate and cystine. Pathologically, the dysfunction of the glutamate aspartate transporter (GLAST) receptor on Müller cells and astrocytes leads to the accumulation of extracellular glutamate, inhibiting system Xc− and ultimately triggering ferroptosis. Notably, intracellular ROS promotes the release of inflammatory factors through the nuclear factor kappaB (NF-κB) pathway, thereby activating microglia and Müller cells. FPN: ferroportin; PAP7: prostate-specific acid phosphatase 7; DFO: desferrioxamine; GSSG: GSH disulfide; NADPH: nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate; PUFAs: polyunsaturated fatty acids; OPA1: optic atrophy 1; MFN1/2: mitofusin 1/2; Drp1: dynamin-related protein 1; GSR: GSH reductase; RSL3: RAS-selective lethal 3; Fer-1: ferrostatin-1; GLT-1: glutamate transporter 1; IL-1β: interleukin-1 beta; TNF: tumor necrosis factor
